Routing observations:
- Option C was rejected for 9 of 10 tickets, with the system explicitly stating “option C is not valid.”
- The sole successful C selection was REQ-2408: a small shipment from the north region, submitted by Regional Ops after a bounced first attempt. Its C label appeared as “regional…”/“regional office.”
- Do not select C by default; it may only be valid for a narrow regional-office case, possibly north-region shipments handled by Regional Ops.
- No evidence yet distinguishes when to choose A (standard queue) versus B (priority desk). Ticket size, request type, region, sender, and urgency wording may affect this, but the failed examples cannot establish the rule because C was selected every time.
- For future tickets, inspect the complete option labels and prefer A or B unless the request clearly matches the validated regional-office pattern.

Routing observations:
- Earlier, C was rejected for 9/10 tickets; the only success was REQ-2408: small north-region shipment from Regional Ops after a bounced first attempt. C was displayed as “regional…”/“regional office.”
- New success: REQ-2410 accepted A for a small east-region claim from Regional Ops. Thus A can be valid for at least this narrow case; do not assume Regional Ops or small size implies C.
- A was rejected for large north shipment (REQ-2412), large south shipment (REQ-2416), small east shipment from Client Services (REQ-2417), and small south claim/shipment from Regional Ops (REQ-2418–2419). The rule is not simply region, size, sender, or request type.
- B was rejected for large east claim/invoice tickets (REQ-2413–2415), including a request explicitly mentioning the regional office. This does not validate B as the priority rule.
- No new C selection was tested, so the regional-office hypothesis remains uncertain. “C (regional office)” may be relevant, but explicit regional-office wording alone did not justify B.
- A prior C success and the new A success suggest multiple interacting attributes (possibly region, size, request type, sender, urgency/history), with too little controlled evidence to isolate the rule.
- For future tickets, inspect complete option labels, including any D option. Avoid repeating A or B merely from superficial similarities; prefer a previously validated pattern only when all key attributes match. Use C only with strong evidence for the exact regional-office routing pattern, and record outcomes to build controlled comparisons.

Routing observations:
- Outcomes are highly attribute-dependent; region, size, sender, request type, and message/history all matter. Do not infer routing from any single attribute.
- A validated: REQ-2410 (small east claim, Regional Ops) and REQ-2421 (small east refund, Regional Ops). Rejected for several north/south or large cases, and REQ-2427 (small east invoice, Regional Ops), so even similar east/Regional Ops tickets can differ.
- C is not a general “regional office” rule. Rejected for REQ-2420 (small north claim), REQ-2424 (large north refund), REQ-2425 (large north shipment), and REQ-2428 (small east shipment), despite explicit Regional Ops or regional-office context. Earlier C success REQ-2408 remains an isolated validated case.
- D validated: REQ-2423 (small east invoice, Partner Accounts) and REQ-2429 (large north claim, Partner Accounts). Rejected for REQ-2422 and REQ-2426 (large south claims), so sender/region/request combinations remain important.
- B has no validated success; earlier large east claim/invoice cases were rejected, including one mentioning the regional office.
- Urgency/history wording may be decisive: “client asking twice” led to A rejection (REQ-2427), while “second attempt, first form bounced” did not make C valid (REQ-2428).
- Always inspect complete option labels, including D. Prefer an exact previously validated combination, not superficial similarity; otherwise treat the choice as uncertain and record the outcome for controlled comparisons.

- Prefer an exact previously validated combination; otherwise treat the choice as uncertain and record results for controlled comparison.

A rejected for REQ-2427 (small east invoice, client asking twice), REQ-2434 (small north invoice, regional-office wording), and REQ-2437 (large east invoice, Field Sales).
- C remains highly selective, not a general regional-office rule. Rejected for REQ-2420, REQ-2424, REQ-2425, REQ-2428, and REQ-2430 (large north invoice, Field Sales), despite regional context in several cases. Earlier C success REQ-2408 remains isolated.
- D validated for REQ-2423 (small east invoice, Partner Accounts), REQ-2429 (large north claim, Partner Accounts), and REQ-2432 (large north claim, Finance Desk). Rejected for REQ-2422, REQ-2426 (large south claims), REQ-2431 (small east shipment, Partner Accounts), and REQ-2436 (small north refund, Partner Accounts).
- B still has no validated success; prior large east claim/invoice cases were rejected.
- REQ-2433 and REQ-2439 show identical small south claim attributes can route to A even with different senders; wording (“paperwork was scanned”) may be relevant. “No rush, confirm receipt” routed A for REQ-2435 but not enough to generalize.
- Urgency/history wording can be decisive: “client asking twice” led to A rejection, while “second attempt, first form bounced” did not make C valid.
